title: property()
summary: Expose a method as an attribute, so a computed value reads like stored state.
description: Lets you start with a plain attribute and add validation or computation later without changing a single caller. That is its real purpose: it removes the reason to write Java-style getters up front.
returns: A descriptor which, on an instance, calls the method on attribute access.

raises.when: Assigning to a property with no setter defined.

examples.title: A computed attribute
Validation on assignment
Read-only by default
examples.output: AttributeError: property 'x' of 'C' object has no setter

real_world_usage: Derived totals, lazily loaded relations, validated fields, and keeping a computed value from drifting out of sync with its inputs.

common_mistakes.fix: Callers assume attribute access is cheap. If it does I/O, make it a method so the cost is visible at the call site.

common_mistakes.mistake: Recursion via self.x inside the property named x
common_mistakes.fix: Store the backing value under a different name, such as self._x.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding a property with a setter that does nothing but assign
common_mistakes.fix: Then it earns nothing. Use a plain attribute until you need the behaviour.

performance_notes: Attribute access through a property is noticeably slower than a plain attribute, because it is a function call. Irrelevant except in hot loops.
security_notes: A setter is a good place to validate, but it is not a boundary — callers can reach the backing attribute directly.
